tasks.task_description: Build a network model of the Great Lakes flow system from Lake Superior to the Atlantic, identify the two control points (Compensating Works of the Soo Locks / St Mary's River, and Moses-Saunders Dam at Cornwall on the St Lawrence), and establish a management model that determines and maintains water levels for the benefit of the stakeholders, with a focused, deeper analysis of Lake Ontario.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) monthly mass conservation in each lake — the water level in month t+1 is set by inflow minus outflow over month t; (2) the river connecting two lakes carries the mass that moves between them, so a lake with one measured outflow has its outflow recoverable as the balance residual; (3) a blank ('---') record means the value was not recorded, not that the flow was zero (a Great-Lakes river cannot run dry for months while the lake above it keeps behaving normally, and the lake-level sheets are complete over the same period); (4) the filled-in months are a representative sample of the underlying process; (5) a single linear volume-to-level sensitivity S = dV/dL per lake over the observed range. The method is a monthly mass-balance (residual) model: it uses only the supplied data, needs no external flow data for the blank rivers, and is self-consistent — re-integrating the balance with the recovered outflow reproduces the observed levels exactly (RMSE 0.0 m over all 276 months), which is the model's core validation. It is a bookkeeping model, not a physical simulation of evaporation or runoff: those enter implicitly through the measured inflows and the level record. Note on the expert consultation: the planned exchanges could not be completed — the expert API failed on every attempt at exchange 1, so exchanges 2-3 were not sent and no expert value entered the model. The mass-balance structure and the operating-band threshold are agent decisions grounded in the dataset and the model's own consistency checks; see interaction_evidence.md.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Chain: Superior -> St Mary's -> Huron -> St Clair -> Erie -> Niagara -> Ontario -> St Lawrence (Ottawa feeds Ontario). For Lake Ontario let L_on(t) be the level (m), F_NIA(t), F_OTT(t) the measured inflows (m^3/s), F_SL(t) the St Lawrence outflow at Cornwall (m^3/s, the controlled column, blank in the data), S_ON the volume-to-level sensitivity (km^3 per m), and KM3 = 30.44*86400/1e9 the km^3 carried in a month by 1 m^3/s. Balance: S_ON*(L_on(t+1)-L_on(t)) = (F_NIA(t)+F_OTT(t)-F_SL(t))*KM3, so the controlled outflow is recovered as F_SL(t) = F_NIA(t)+F_OTT(t) - S_ON*(L_on(t+1)-L_on(t))/KM3. S_ON is the only empirical parameter. Parameter table: S_ON = 20, interval [15, 25], source: calibrated so implied storage at the 2000-2022 mean level (74.82 m) matches the lake's known contents (~1620 km^3), i.e. S_ON ~ 1620/74.8 ~ 21.6; value 20 used as base and 12/15/25/30 swept (result insensitive: recovered outflow mean moves <0.1% across the range). Level reconstruction: L(t+1) = L(t) + (F_NIA(t)+F_OTT(t)-F_SL(t))*KM3/S_ON. Upstream connecting flows (St Mary's, St Clair, Detroit) are absent from the sheets and are estimated as the upstream lake's volume change over its own sensitivity; the St Mary's estimate ranges 520-1250 m^3/s as S_SUPERIOR ranges 25-60 km^3/m. Sensitivity: a sustained fractional change d in the Cornwall outflow moves the Ontario level by -d*mean(F_SL)*KM3/S_ON per month (S_ON=20: -0.106 m for d=0.1, -1.06 m for d=1.0). The Ontario-level elasticity to a 1 m^3/s change in inflow is 2.62e-4 m (Niagara) and 5.3e-5 m (Ottawa) from an OLS on the 23-year record (R^2 = 0.48).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recovered Cornwall outflow: mean 8066 m^3/s, std 1538, range 3618-13984, correlated with total inflow (r = 0.71) with a spring peak (May mean 9255 m^3/s) and autumn low (Dec 7315 m^3/s). Model consistency: re-integrating the balance with the recovered outflow reproduces the observed level exactly (RMSE 0.0 m, all months); the 23-year interannual level std is only 0.29 m, so the lake is a well-damped system. 2017: recorded levels ran 74.62 (Jan) to 75.81 m (Jun); 5 of 12 months sat above the 90th percentile (75.18 m) and none below the 10th (74.49 m), and the 2017 mean implied outflow (9562 m^3/s) was ~19% above the 23-year mean — i.e. 2017 was a high-water, high-release year in which the dam drained the lake quickly after the spring peak to keep it out of the flood band. Verdict on the subproblem 'would new controls be satisfactory or better in 2017': the model reproduces the 2017 record exactly, and the 2017 operating point kept the lake above the shipping floor in every month while shedding the spring surge, so it was satisfactory for shipping and flood stakeholders; a simple fixed-seasonal-outflow policy (a management baseline) drifts ~9.6 m in 2017 and is far worse, confirming that active, inflow-responsive control (what the model's recovered outflow is) is what keeps the level in the band. Limitations and biases: (a) the model is a residual — it defines F_SL so as to fit the level, so its 'prediction' of the level is exact by construction and its real content is the recovered outflow and its seasonality, not a forecast; (b) S_ON is externally calibrated, so the absolute outflow magnitude carries the uncertainty of that constant (small over the swept range, but the lake's true dV/dL varies with level); (c) the blank St Mary's / St Clair / Detroit / St Lawrence sheets mean the upstream chain is reconstructed, not observed, and the St Mary's estimate is S_SUPERIOR-sensitive; (d) evaporation, precipitation and basin runoff enter only through the measured inflow and level, so a regime shift (e.g. a drier spring) is captured only insofar as it shows up in those series; (e) thresholds (10th/90th percentile) are data-driven, not the IJC's published navigability targets, so the stakeholder verdict is framed against the historical operating band rather than the regulatory one.
